title: After Finishing My Study Abroad at the University of Pennsylvania
paragraphs: From March to June 2007, for about three months, I took part in clinical clerkships at the University of Pennsylvania School of Medicine in Philadelphia. In this program, you choose three departments and do a four-week clerkship in each, participating in the same way as the local medical students. The three departments I was assigned to were pediatric cardiology, urology, and the spine team of orthopedic surgery.

The University of Pennsylvania has several hospitals that function like university hospitals, so the clerkship sites varied by department, and in the end I did clerkships at four hospitals in total. These three months were truly a time when I studied hard, played hard, and had a lot of fun. My first clerkship, in pediatric cardiology, was at The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP). On the medicine inpatient ward, the attending rounds were the main event of the day, and unlike in Japan, everyone does them together every day for several hours. At that time, the resident in training presents their patients to the attending physician, and then there is a discussion. The presentations were so fast that on the first day I could hardly understand anything, and I remember the shock well. The problem was not only the speed. Many abbreviations specific to pediatric cardiology were used, so it was a doubly foreign-language world. Even so, after a few days I got used to both the speed and the abbreviations to some extent, and strangely enough I became able to understand roughly the content. I had my own patients, did my own rounds every morning, and then gave a presentation at the attending rounds. Sometimes my presentations were praised, and I felt as though I had become a member of the team. Since it was my first department, I was still confused, but over these four weeks I realised that nothing starts unless you move on your own, and that conversely, if you are proactive, everyone teaches you very kindly. I think I was able to make use of that in my later clerkships.

My second clerkship was urology. Over the four weeks, in addition to CHOP, I did clerkships at the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania (HUP) and Pennsylvania Hospital. What shocked me here was the length of the clerkship hours. It was not unusual to gather before 6 a.m. for rounds, spend the day in the operating room afterward, and finish around 8 p.m. Depending on the hospital, some doctors start rounds around 5 a.m., so students and residents have to go to the hospital at 4:30 and finish rounds for their patients. It was a little hard, of course, but it was fun to be allowed to do various things when assisting in surgery, and many of the allied health staff were interesting people and the atmosphere in the operating room was good, so every day was fulfilling. I introduced myself to the nurses every time, so by the second day many of them remembered my name, and when I parted from them after a week I felt somewhat sad. My last clerkship was the spine team of orthopedic surgery. I did it at Penn Presbyterian Medical Center and HUP, but since it was my second surgical clerkship, I knew my way around the operating room and was less confused. I judged that four weeks of spine alone would be a little lacking in interest, so I asked the doctor and also did a clerkship with the joint team. As clerkships become familiar, you gain much more leeway, and I even explained various things in a senior-like manner to a first-year student who had come for a clerkship from South Carolina. What impressed me most here was that one doctor let me do a procedure during surgery that would normally never be given to a student, and said, "You are the only medical student in the world who has done this." Later he told me, "You did that so calmly that you will surely be a good surgeon," and although I thought it was an exaggeration, I was truly happy. In addition to the hospital clerkships above, my everyday life was also very enjoyable. There were many international students in the dormitory, so I had the chance to make friends with people from European countries. In the latter two departments, the clerkships continued from early morning until late at night, so there were many days when I just ate and slept after getting home, but on weekends I went out to various places with them and enjoyed myself. Toward the end, weekends were no longer enough, and I lived an unusual life: eating dinner, going to a movie, then going out for drinks, and coming back at 2 a.m. with a 6:30 a.m. meeting time the next day. The parting was hard because we had enjoyed ourselves so much, but I plan to keep in touch and hope to see them again. Talking with them, I could learn how people from other countries see America, which was very interesting. These three months went by really quickly, but I had so many experiences that I cannot write them all here, and I was greatly influenced by them. I sincerely thank the professors and administrative staff who made this valuable experience possible, and everyone else who helped me.
